s: B. Constitutional interpretation.
Constitutional argument draws on a recognized set of "modalities" (the term is Philip Bobbitt's).
A well-made argument names the modality it relies on and explains why it should control.
Text.
The words of the provision, read in context and with attention to their ordinary and legal meaning when adopted.
Textual arguments are strongest where the text is specific (the President must be thirty-five) and weakest where it is open-textured ("due process," "unreasonable searches").
Original meaning and history.
Founding-era dictionaries, debates, ratification materials, and early practice.
Original public meaning originalism asks what a reasonable reader at ratification would have understood; older original intent approaches asked what the drafters meant.
The Court has increasingly relied on history and tradition, most prominently in Heller, Bruen, Dobbs and Kennedy v. Bremerton.
Structure.
Inferences from the relationships the Constitution sets up.
Examples are federalism (Printz), separation of powers (Chadha), and the implied immunity of federal instrumentalities from state taxation (McCulloch).
Precedent.
Stare decisis promotes stability and reliance.
The Court treats it as a "principle of policy," weakest in constitutional cases.
When deciding whether to overrule, it weighs the quality of the reasoning, workability, consistency with related decisions, later developments, and reliance (Dobbs; Janus; Ramos).
Prudential and consequential arguments.
Administrability, institutional competence, and the practical effects of a rule.
Ethos and tradition.
Arguments from the nation's deeply rooted traditions or evolving moral commitments.
These are most visible in substantive due process (Glucksberg, Obergefell), and their legitimacy is sharply contested.
The method a judge chooses often decides the case.
In Dobbs the majority's history-and-tradition test, applied to abortion, produced the opposite answer from the dissent's precedent-and-liberty analysis.
Overruling precedent: factors the Court considers.
The nature of the error: how wrong was the decision?
The quality of the reasoning.
Workability of the rule it established.
Effect on other areas of law (doctrinal coherence).
Reliance interests, especially concrete property and contract reliance.
